newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden banks sector seen calmer after merger fails.
newsitem.headline: Sweden banks sector seen calmer after merger fails.

text.p: Sweden's bank sector is headed for a temporary reprieve in coming months after a six month frenzy of corporate speculation was stopped dead on Monday when a much expected merger failed to proceed.

Two of Sweden's big four banks, commercial S-E-Banken and state-controlled Nordbanken, surprised the market on Monday, announcing merger talks that have fuelled shares in the bank sector in recent months were over.

The end of the deal was seen limiting further possible merger and takeover activity in the sector with some analysts suggesting Swedish banks may start to look regionally, possibly to Denmark, or to the insurance sector for new moves.
"This does not remove the desirability for major restructuring in the banking sector in Sweden but I think it will be quiet for a while," banking analyst Peter Thorn from Paribas told Reuters.
Swedish banks shares have surged since last autumn on speculation about sector restructuring which is expected to take place before Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

With the EMU seen pitting Swedish banks against much larger competitors, falling interest rates, better economic growth forecast and improving corporate results, analysts said the time was ripe for rationalising Sweden's finance sector.
On these expectations, the banking sector index has surged around 43 percent since early September compared to an overall rise in the Stockholm bourse's general index of 28 percent.
"The end of this merger will take some of the heat out of the merger frenzy but the market will probably maintain the price levels we see now," Fiba analyst Jan Dworsky said.

"It was a spectacular performance last year driven by sharply lower interest rates and merger activities speculation but now it is only down to interest rates. It is hard to see any further performance from these levels in this sector."
During Monday trade the bank sector index slipped back over two percent while the overall market was 0.12 percent lower.
Speculation over mergers and acquisitions among Swedish banks took off last September with rumours over a possible merger between S-E-Banken and Handelsbanken.
Such a big merger was seen having strong potential for cost-cutting with volume advantages which, with lending margins under pressure, would be a welcome route to higher profits.

But the rumours bit the dust when Handelsbanken barged its way into negotiations on a merger between insurer Skandia and mortgage bank Stadshypotek, making a 22.9 billion crowns ($3.13 billion)cash bid for Stadshypotek.
Handelsbanken, Sweden's largest bank by assets, received the government nod for its bid for Stadshypotek, which is 34 percent state owned, and the deal should be final this month.
Interest from Sweden's fourth big bank, Swedbank in key rural player Foreningsbanken also seemed shortlived when the farmers' association rebuffed its advances.
With these players sidelined, the focus fell on Nordbanken which is 59 percent owned by the state.
Analysts expected the sale of tranches to institutional shareholders or possibly a second share buyback scheme in a year or so, mirroring a successful scheme in late 1996.
But although some speculation was expected to continue to fizz in the market, it was seen as far lower key.
"With two rebuffed deals, S-E-Banken won't be jumping into more discussions without a more sober attitude," said Thorn. ($1=7.31 crowns)
